notes.meaning: The poet cries out in shock that God Himself has covered Jerusalem, called the Daughter of Zion, with a dark cloud of anger. The city once knew the bright cloud of God's glory, but now the cloud means judgment. She has been thrown down from the heights of honor to the lowest misery. God's "footstool" is the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest in the temple that stood for His presence, and even this He did not spare.

Without pity God has swallowed up the homes and strong cities of Judah. This begins a long list of "He has" lines. The Babylonian army did the damage, but the poet wants us to see God's hand behind it. The kingdom and its princes were "defiled," handed over to unholy enemies, after the people had first defiled themselves with idols.

A "horn" was a picture of strength and glory, and God has cut off all of Israel's. He has pulled back His right hand, the help He used to give against their enemies. His anger burned like a fire that catches a house on every side at once.

God is pictured as an archer who bends His bow and aims at His own people. The usual picture of God fighting for Israel is turned around. Those "pleasing to the eye" were the young, the beautiful, and the leaders, the flower of the people. Still, God is not truly His people's enemy, even when He corrects them in anger.

The Lord has acted "like an enemy," swallowing up even the grand, well-guarded palaces. The poet repeats this so the people will look past the Babylonians to God's judgment. With all their defenses gone, mourning grew and grew. In the original, "mourning and lamentation" are two words that sound alike, which makes the sorrow ring louder.

God tore down His temple as easily as a farmer takes down a little shelter in his garden. The places where people met to worship are gone. With the temple fallen, the feasts and Sabbaths stopped, and those who had not honored those holy days lost them. King and priest were cast off too, likely King Zedekiah and the high priest Seraiah.

God has rejected His own altar and sanctuary, the holy place of worship. Enemy soldiers now shout in the temple, as loud as worshipers once sang at the feasts. The sad contrast shows how far things have fallen. God allowed this because His people had already made the temple unclean by their sins.

Jerusalem's wall did not fall by chance. God had decided to bring it down. In those days a measuring line was used to mark what to tear down, not only what to build, so the ruin was careful and complete. The walls are pictured as mourning, showing that the grief was so great even stones seemed to share it.

The city gates lie buried in rubble and their bars are broken. Gates are no help when God takes away His protection. The king and princes are captives in foreign lands. God's law is no longer read or kept, and the prophets get no message from God. That silence was one of the saddest losses of all.

The leaders who once sat as judges now sit on the ground in silence, with dust on their heads and rough sackcloth on their bodies. These were signs of deep mourning. The young women, once proud of their looks, bow their heads to the ground. Old and young together stand for the whole city in grief. As one writer puts it, small griefs talk, but great ones are silent.

Now the prophet speaks of his own sorrow. He has cried until his eyes give out, and his insides feel torn apart. Most of all he grieves for the little children fainting from hunger in the streets during the long siege. Jeremiah himself was treated better than most, yet he mourned for his people as if he were the one suffering most.
Hungry children ask their mothers for bread and wine, but there is none. Hunger kills them as surely as a sword. Some die right in their mothers' arms. It is a scene meant to break the hardest heart.

The prophet wants to comfort Jerusalem but cannot find the words. People often comfort sufferers by saying others have had it worse, or that things can be fixed. Neither is true here. No city has suffered like this, and her wound is as wide and deep as the sea.

The false prophets told the people only pleasant things. They never pointed out their sins, which might have led them to turn back to God and so escape captivity. Their soothing messages ended up bringing a far heavier "burden" of disaster. True servants of God show people their sin so they can repent and find mercy.

People passing by clap, hiss, and shake their heads at the ruined city. They mock her with her own proud words from the Psalms: "the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth." Her beauty came from the gifts God had given her. Laughing at someone else's misery is a real sin and adds pain to the hurting.

Jerusalem's enemies open their mouths wide like hungry beasts and grind their teeth in hatred. They boast that they have swallowed her up, the day they had long hoped for. But enemies of God's people often mistake a hard blow for the end. They will be proved wrong.

The poet turns from the gloating enemies to God. The Lord did what He had planned. He kept the warnings He gave long ago through Moses, that disobedience would bring judgment. The enemies only had power because God gave it to them. This verse matches verse 8: what God announced, He carried out.

The people's hearts cry out to the Lord. The city wall, standing for the whole city, is called on to weep like a river, day and night, without rest. Some fear this cry came more from pain than from real sorrow for sin, so they are urged to keep crying until their hard hearts are softened.

Get up in the night and pray, the prophet says. Pour out your heart like water before God, and lift your hands to Him, a sign of prayer. Ask Him at least to spare your starving children. Prayer is the cure for every hurt, even the deepest.

Jerusalem begs God to look at what has happened to His own chosen people. Mothers have eaten their children, as God's law had warned would happen if the people turned away (Deuteronomy 28:53). Priests and prophets have been killed in the very temple. These horrors are laid before God to move Him to mercy.

Young and old lie dead together in the streets. The sword spared no age and no one, men or women. The city says God has done this in His anger. This is not to argue with God. It helps the people see they are dealing with Him, so they can admit their sin and ask for mercy.

Crowds of worshipers used to pour into Jerusalem for the great feasts. Now God has called in crowds of enemies from every side instead. No one escaped. The children the city lovingly raised have been destroyed. The enemy struck the blow, but God was the one behind it.
